title: Automation architecture and Flow/Apex boundaries
objectives: Place automation architecture on the official which-tool spectrum: formula, validation, approval, Flow, then Apex when Flow cannot meet the need.
Draw Flow versus Apex boundaries using maintainability (Easy), save-order participation, bulkification, and callout timing—not a preference for code.
Detect duplicate automation on the same object as an architecture defect, not a feature.
Cite the Apex order-of-execution guide rather than reciting an unofficial step list from memory.
diagnostic_question: A same-record status stamp, a cross-object roll-up with branching, a callout, and an approval chain all land on Opportunity. Before reading, which belong in formula, validation, approval, before-save Flow, after-save Flow, or Apex—and what evidence would move one item across the Flow/Apex boundary?
definition: Salesforce automation architecture is the designed set of formula fields, validation rules, approval processes, Flow, and Apex that implement business logic on a save or a user action. Official Help tells you to pick the simplest tool that meets the requirement and to use Apex when Flow cannot. Flow and Apex both participate in the documented record save order, so two cooks on the same pan (duplicate automation) is a defect. ([Which Tool](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.process_which_tool.htm); [Easy Overview](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/easy-overview.html); [Order of Execution](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm))
why_it_matters: Interviewers listen for 'Flow first unless Flow cannot,' plus save-order awareness, plus Easy maintainability. A trigger farm that reprints what a before-save Flow already does fails Easy even if it compiles. A Flow that performs a synchronous callout from a trigger-shaped path fails the same boundary from the other side. Governors and exact Flow limits belong to cited Limits docs, not folklore.
sixty_second_explanation: Treat automation like a restaurant kitchen brigade. Formula and validation are the printed recipe cards at the station. Approvals are the manager's sign-off on a plate. Record-triggered Flow is the line cook following a visible recipe. Apex is the pastry chef for techniques the recipe cards cannot express. The pass window is the official order of execution: every ticket hits the window in a documented sequence. Two cooks seasoning the same pan is not 'resilience'—it is a race. Easy asks whether the night shift can still read the recipe.
deeper_explanation: Salesforce Help on choosing the right automation tool places formula fields, validation rules, approval processes, Flow, and Apex on one spectrum. Use the simplest tool that works. Use Apex when you need something a flow cannot do or you need more flexibility than a flow provides. ([Which Tool](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.process_which_tool.htm))

Well-Architected Easy treats healthy automation as efficiency plus data integrity, and it warns that a design only a programmer can maintain is not Easy. Automation architecture is therefore an ownership decision as much as a tool decision. ([Easy Overview](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/easy-overview.html))

The Apex Developer Guide publishes Triggers and Order of Execution: system validation, before-save record-triggered flows, before triggers, custom validation rules, duplicate rules, after triggers, assignment rules, auto-response, workflow (legacy), processes (legacy), escalation, after-save flows, roll-up summaries, and later steps such as sharing recalculation and outbound messages appear in that documented sequence. Recite from the current page; do not memorize an unofficial blog numbering. ([Order of Execution](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm))

Boundary heuristics for interviews (always re-check the which-tool page): same-record field updates often fit before-save Flow; user-facing screens and orchestrated work fit screen or autolaunched Flow; approvals have their own engine (classic versus Flow approval processes—confirm current Help); Apex for complex transactions, reusable services, callouts (not synchronous HTTP from a trigger), and cases Flow cannot express. Exact Flow CPU, DML, or element caps: cite current Limits documentation or mark Needs verification.
Workflow Rules and Process Builder are retired/legacy on the save-order page. New architecture should not add them. Duplicate Flow plus trigger on the same entry condition is the two-cooks defect.

mental_model.analogy: A restaurant kitchen brigade: printed recipe cards are formula and validation; manager sign-off is approval; line cooks following visible recipes are Flow; the pastry chef is Apex; the pass window is the official order of execution; two cooks seasoning one pan is duplicate automation.
useful_mapping: formula / validation → printed cards at the station
approval process → manager sign-off before the plate leaves
before-save Flow → seasoning the pan before it hits the window
after-save Flow → garnish and side tickets after the plate is up
Apex → pastry technique the cards cannot express
order of execution → the pass window sequence
duplicate Flow + trigger → two cooks, one pan
where_it_breaks: A kitchen has one pass; Salesforce save order includes legacy workflow and process steps you should not add to.
Apex callouts cannot be synchronous from a trigger the way a pastry chef can wait on an oven—timing is a platform rule.
The analogy does not encode governor-limit numbers; cite Limits docs.
Easy ownership may prefer Flow even when Apex would be 'faster for a specialist.'

teach_back_prompt: Explain formula, validation, approval, Flow, and Apex with the kitchen brigade, then name where the pass-window analogy breaks on callouts and legacy tools.

review_schedule.prompt: From memory, recite the which-tool order and the Apex-when-Flow-cannot rule.
Place four LAB_ Opportunity needs on the spectrum without looking.
Explain before-save versus after-save Flow using the order-of-execution page, not a blog.
Diagnose two cooks on one pan: Flow and trigger on the same entry.
Two-minute interview: Flow/Apex boundary, Easy ownership, no invented Flow limits.

claims.claim: Help instructs builders to choose the simplest automation tool that meets the requirement, spanning formula fields, validation rules, approval processes, Flow, and Apex. Use Apex when a flow cannot do the work or more flexibility than a flow provides is required.
claims.validation: Which Automation Tool Do I Use? Help.

claims.claim: Easy architectures require maintainable automation. A design that only a programmer can own can fail Easy even if it is technically reliable.

Record-triggered flows and Apex triggers participate in a documented order of execution that includes before-save flows, before triggers, validation rules, after triggers, and after-save flows among other platform steps.
Apex executes transaction control on the Salesforce server. Callouts initiated from trigger context must run asynchronously from the triggering DML.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: I pick the simplest tool on the official spectrum. Flow first when the owning team can maintain it. Apex when Flow cannot, or for a coded service or async callout. I design one automation per entry condition because save order is a pass window, not a place for two cooks.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: Same-record updates often go before-save Flow. Approvals stay on the approval engine. I open the order-of-execution page instead of reciting a blog. I refuse a new Workflow Rule. I refuse synchronous HTTP from a trigger. Easy can fail a clever trigger farm. I do not invent Flow limit numbers.

terminology.plain: The planned mix of declarative and programmatic logic for a process.
terminology.precise: An intentional map of formula, validation, approval, Flow, and Apex per object and entry condition, aligned to the which-tool spectrum and Easy maintainability.
terminology.example: LAB_Opportunity: validation for required stage reasons, before-save Flow for a status stamp, one after-save Flow for tasks, no extra trigger.
terminology.non_example: Five triggers and three flows all on Opportunity update with overlapping criteria.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: A single Flow interview debug: runtime of one tool, not the architecture.
terminology.boundary: AUTO-001 teaches tool choice in more product depth; this lesson is the architect boundary.

terminology.plain: When the recipe cards are enough versus when you need the pastry chef.
terminology.precise: Official rule: use Apex when a flow cannot do the work or you need more flexibility than a flow provides—plus Easy ownership of whoever maintains it.
terminology.example: Complex multi-object splitting with a callout pattern that Flow cannot express cleanly → Apex service.
terminology.non_example: Writing Apex for a same-record field stamp a before-save Flow already covers.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Invocable Apex inside Flow: a hybrid, not a reason to skip the boundary question.
terminology.boundary: Exact Flow capability matrix is versioned; reverify Help rather than memorizing an unofficial list.

terminology.plain: Flow that updates the same record before it is committed.
terminology.precise: A record-triggered flow that runs in the before-save portion of the order of execution, suited to same-record field updates without a DML in that path.
terminology.example: Stamp LAB_Status__c on Opportunity before insert/update.
terminology.non_example: Creating child tasks in before-save—that needs after-save or another path.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Before Apex trigger: same window family, different owner skill.

terminology.plain: Flow that runs after the record is saved, for extra work.
terminology.precise: A record-triggered flow later in the save order, used when you need the committed record id or additional DML such as related records.
terminology.example: Create a LAB_Task after Opportunity reaches a stage.
terminology.non_example: A same-record field update that could have been before-save and now risks recursion.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: After Apex trigger: overlapping window; pick one owner per concern.
terminology.boundary: Recursion and re-entry are design risks; test them.

terminology.plain: The documented sequence of the save pass window.
terminology.precise: The Apex Developer Guide list of what runs on insert/update, including before-save flows, triggers, validation rules, after-save flows, and later platform steps. Use the current page as source of truth.
terminology.example: Explaining why a validation rule sees values already changed by before-save Flow.
terminology.non_example: An unofficial 21-step blog printed as if it were the guide.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Flow interview order inside one Flow: different from the record save order.
terminology.boundary: Legacy workflow and process builder still appear as steps; do not add new ones.

terminology.plain: Two cooks seasoning the same pan.
terminology.precise: Two or more automations (Flow, trigger, legacy process) implementing the same entry condition or mutating the same field without a single owner.
terminology.example: Process Builder leftover plus a new record-triggered Flow both setting LAB_Status__c.
terminology.non_example: A validation rule plus a Flow that only creates a task—different jobs.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Invocable Apex reused by one Flow: composition, if there is a single orchestrator.
terminology.boundary: Inventory existing automation before adding another.

when_to_use: When an interview asks you to design Salesforce automation architecture and defend Flow versus Apex boundaries.
When a same-record update, an approval, a related-record create, and a callout compete on one object.
When you discover duplicate Flow and trigger logic on the same entry condition (two cooks).
When a programmer-only trigger farm would fail Easy even though it compiles.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this lesson as a substitute for AUTO-001 product walkthroughs of every Flow type, or for Apex governor catalogs (APEX-007).
Do not invent Flow element or CPU limit numbers; cite current Limits documentation.
Do not add new Workflow Rules or Process Builder as if they were current architecture.
Do not put a synchronous HTTP callout in a trigger and call it automation architecture.
configuration_or_code_location: Setup → Flows, Approval Processes, Validation Rules, Formula fields.
Setup → Apex Triggers / Apex Classes for coded automation.
Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution.
Disposable sandbox only; synthetic LAB_ objects.

worked_example.scenario: LAB_Opportunity needs: (1) stamp a status field on the same record, (2) require a lost reason, (3) manager approval above a threshold, (4) create a task after save, (5) notify an external credit service. A developer starts a single before-and-after trigger for all five. Sandbox only.

decisions.decision: Validation rule for lost reason; before-save Flow for the stamp; approval process for the threshold; after-save Flow for the task.
decisions.because: Which-tool says simplest tool; these are in Flow/declarative reach.
decisions.rejected: One Apex trigger for all five

decisions.decision: Apex (async) only for the credit callout, invoked from a path that is not a synchronous trigger HTTP call.
decisions.because: Trigger context cannot wait on a synchronous callout; Apex is justified where Flow plus platform events or async Apex is the documented pattern.
decisions.rejected: HTTP callout inside before insert trigger

decisions.decision: Do not also keep a leftover Process Builder on the same stamp field.
decisions.because: Two cooks on one pan plus legacy on the save-order page.
decisions.rejected: Add Flow 'just for now' beside Process Builder

configuration_or_code: Build LAB_ declarative pieces in sandbox; keep credit callout as a stubbed async class.
worked_example.output: A written automation map with one owner per concern and Apex only on the callout boundary.
verification: No overlapping Flow and trigger on the stamp field.
Callout is not synchronous from a trigger.
Which-tool rationale is written for each of the five needs.
worked_example.self_explanation: I used the spectrum, not a trigger preference. The pass window cannot host two cooks. Callouts are async.

hands_on_lab.environment: Disposable sandbox with synthetic LAB_Opportunity or a custom LAB_ object.
starting_state_checks: You can create a validation rule and a record-triggered Flow.
You will not deploy to production.
steps: Inventory existing automation on the LAB_ object (flows, triggers, approval, validation, legacy processes).
Implement a same-record stamp with before-save Flow and a validation rule for a required reason—no Apex.
Open the official order-of-execution page and write which step your Flow occupies.
Write why a credit-check callout would not go in that Flow or in a synchronous trigger.
guided_completion: If you created both a trigger and a Flow for the stamp, delete one.
If you quoted a Flow limit number, replace it with a Limits-doc citation or Needs verification.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Add an after-save Flow that creates a LAB_Task and explain why that DML was not done before-save.
evidence: Screenshot or retrieve of the Flow and validation rule (LAB_ names).
A one-paragraph save-order citation in your own words.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Deactivate LAB_ flows and delete lab Apex if you created any.
Do not leave duplicate automation in a shared sandbox.
hands_on_lab.limitations: This lab does not prove governor headroom or Flow interview limits.

decision_table.signal: A calculated value displayed on the record or a simple same-record constraint.
decision_table.choose: Formula field or validation rule first.
decision_table.not: An Apex trigger or after-save Flow that only reprints the formula.
decision_table.why: Which-tool starts with the simplest declarative tools.

decision_table.signal: A same-record field update the admin team can own, no callout.
decision_table.not: A before trigger 'because architects write Apex,' or after-save DML to the same record without a reason.
decision_table.why: Before-save Flow sits early in the official save order and avoids extra DML for same-row updates.

decision_table.choose: Approval process (confirm classic versus Flow approvals in current Help).
decision_table.not: A custom Apex state machine that reimplements approvals without a documented gap.
decision_table.why: Which-tool includes approvals as their own engine.

decision_table.signal: Flow cannot express the transaction, reusable service, or you need a trigger-safe async callout.
decision_table.choose: Apex (invocable, trigger, or async job) with a written why Flow cannot.
decision_table.not: Synchronous HTTP from a trigger, or Apex for a stamp Flow already covers.
decision_table.why: Help: Apex when Flow cannot or more flexibility is required; trigger callouts must be async.

decision_table.signal: A second Flow, trigger, or legacy process already mutates the same field on the same entry.
decision_table.choose: Consolidate to one orchestrator; retire the duplicate.
decision_table.why: Save order will run both; Easy maintainability and data integrity fail.

limitations: Does not catalog every Flow element.
Legacy workflow/process steps still run if present; do not add new ones.
Flow Approval Processes feature gates need current Help.
security_notes: Automation runs in a user or system context depending on the tool; threat-model who it runs as (ARCH-004).
Do not hard-code secrets in Flow or Apex.
Callouts use named credentials, not passwords in formulas.

troubleshooting.symptom: A field value flips twice on one save.
check: Inventory Flow, trigger, and legacy process on that field

troubleshooting.symptom: Validation rule fires on a value you thought Flow already set.
check: Whether the Flow is after-save (too late) versus before-save

troubleshooting.symptom: Callout error from a trigger save.
check: Whether the callout is synchronous in trigger context
Move to async Apex or a non-trigger entry

production_notes: Inventory production automation before go-live; duplicates are incidents waiting to happen.
Retire legacy processes as a controlled project, not a silent add-on.
Reverify order of execution if you depend on a specific step number.

options.B: Whenever an architect is on the team

mcqs.rationale: Which Automation Tool Do I Use? places Apex after Flow for those reasons.

distractor_explanations.C: Validation remains the simplest tool for many constraints.

mcqs.prompt: Which tools sit on the official automation spectrum in this lesson?

options.A: Formula fields, validation rules, approval processes, Flow, and Apex

mcqs.prompt: Where should you look for the save-order sequence of flows and triggers?

options.A: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution
options.B: An unofficial 21-step blog as the system of record

distractor_explanations.B: Blogs drift; the guide is official.
distractor_explanations.D: Wrong pillar for the sequence list.

mcqs.prompt: Best first tool for a same-record status stamp the admin team will own?

options.B: Synchronous HTTP from a before trigger

mcqs.rationale: Simplest automation that fits; before-save avoids extra DML for same-row updates.

mcqs.prompt: A programmer-only trigger farm replaces a readable Flow the admins owned. Which Well-Architected risk?

options.A: It can fail Easy even if it compiles
options.D: Easy is only about button colors

mcqs.rationale: Easy Overview: programmer-only designs can fail Easy.

distractor_explanations.C: Apex is allowed when Flow cannot.

mcqs.prompt: Synchronous HTTP callout from a before-insert trigger. Architect verdict?

options.A: Do not; callouts from trigger context must be asynchronous
options.D: The same as a formula field

mcqs.rationale: Trigger DML cannot wait on a synchronous callout; use async Apex or another pattern.

distractor_explanations.B: Real-time UI callouts are a different entry (often LWC plus Apex), not trigger HTTP.
distractor_explanations.C: OOE does not bless sync trigger callouts.

mcqs.prompt: A leftover Process Builder and a new record-triggered Flow both set the same field. What is the defect?

options.A: Duplicate automation—two cooks on one pan; consolidate and retire legacy

mcqs.rationale: Save order will run both; Easy and data integrity suffer.

mcqs.prompt: Need a manager approval chain on a discount. First architecture choice?

options.A: Approval process (confirm classic vs Flow approvals in current Help)
options.B: A before-save Flow that emails a random user

mcqs.rationale: Which-tool includes approvals as the engine for that job.

mcqs.prompt: Validation fires on a value you expected Flow to set. Likely save-order issue?

options.A: The Flow is after-save, so validation already ran; use before-save for same-record values validation must see
options.B: Validation never runs if any Flow exists

mcqs.rationale: Order of execution places before-save flows and before triggers before custom validation; after-save is later.

mcqs.prompt: A teammate quotes 'Flow maxes at 47 elements.' Response?

options.A: Do not invent numbers; cite current Limits documentation or mark Needs verification
options.C: It is the order-of-execution step count

mcqs.rationale: This handbook forbids invented scale numbers.

options.A: Before-save updates the same record before commit; after-save is later and can do extra DML such as related records

distractor_explanations.C: After-save is after validation and after commit of the original save path.
distractor_explanations.D: Callouts do not belong in before-save.

mcqs.prompt: Invocable Apex called from Flow versus a standalone overlapping trigger?

options.A: Invocable Apex can be a single orchestrated hybrid; a second trigger on the same entry is duplicate automation unless justified

mcqs.rationale: Composition under one Flow is different from two independent mutators.

distractor_explanations.B: Hybrids are valid when Flow cannot do a piece.

interview_questions.question: How do you choose between Flow and Apex on a Salesforce automation architecture?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Simplest tool that works. Flow when the owning team can maintain it. Apex when Flow cannot, or for a coded service or async callout. I write the why.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start from which-tool Help, not from a language preference. Same-record stamps often go before-save Flow. Approvals stay on the approval engine. I inventory existing automations so I do not add a second cook. Easy can fail a clever trigger farm. I do not invent Flow limits.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Opportunity stamp in before-save Flow; credit check in async Apex.
tradeoffs: One Flow versus Flow plus invocable
follow_ups: What if Flow hits a documented limit?
weak_answer_warnings: Apex always because we are architects

interview_questions.question: Why does order of execution matter to automation architecture?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Flows, triggers, and validation share one save pass. Before-save work is visible to validation; after-save is too late for that. Duplicates both run.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I open the Developer Guide page rather than reciting a blog. I place same-record updates before validation when they must be seen. I explain why two automations on one field flicker. I mention leftover workflow as a ghost cook. I do not claim a step number without the current page.
interview_questions.example: After-save Flow sets a field validation already rejected.
tradeoffs: Before-save speed vs after-save DML needs
One page of truth vs tribal memory
follow_ups: Where do assignment rules sit? (Look it up.)

interview_questions.question: Five Opportunity needs including a callout. A developer wants one trigger. Respond.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Split them. Validation, before-save Flow, approval, after-save Flow, and async Apex for the callout. Not one trigger, and not sync HTTP in before insert.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I map each need to which-tool. I refuse a god trigger because Easy and testing suffer. The callout is the real Apex justification. I inventory leftover Process Builder on the stamp field. I keep named credentials out of the Flow formula.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Opportunity worked example in this lesson.
tradeoffs: One class vs several declarative tools
Real-time UI callout vs trigger-time async
follow_ups: Could the callout be user-button plus LWC?
How do you test the Flow?

interview_questions.question: Admins owned a Flow. A rewrite in undocumented Apex 'for performance' is proposed with no measured limit. Answer.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Show evidence of a documented limit first. Easy can fail if admins must still own the rule. I will not invent a Flow cap to justify Apex.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: If current Limits docs show Flow cannot meet a measured NFR, Apex is justified and I still want tests and a readable service. If the issue is unselective queries, that is ARCH-003, not 'Flow is slow.' I would consider invocable Apex under the Flow so ownership stays at the orchestrator.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ status Flow replaced by a 2,000-line trigger with no CPU measurement.
follow_ups: What would you measure in a volume sandbox?

interview_questions.question: A field flips twice on one user save. How do you debug?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Inventory every Flow, trigger, and legacy process on that field. Two cooks. Do not start with 'Salesforce bug.'
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use debug logs or Flow interviews to see both writers. I check before versus after fighting, and recursion from after-save DML. I retire the duplicate rather than adding a third 'fixer' Flow. I cite order of execution to explain the sequence to the team.
interview_questions.example: Process Builder leftover plus new record-triggered Flow on LAB_Status__c.
tradeoffs: Retire legacy now vs freeze and migrate
One orchestrator vs many small flows
follow_ups: How do you find inactive but still-invoked processes?
Could a managed package be the second cook?
weak_answer_warnings: Adding another Flow to overwrite the overwrite

interview_questions.question: Save fails with a callout-related error from a trigger. What do you check first?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Whether the callout is synchronous in trigger context. Move it async. Do not first blame the remote URL.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I look at the stack: before/after trigger, @future/Queueable, named credential. I consider a user-driven LWC plus Apex if the NFR is request-reply on a button (ARCH-006). I still keep secrets out of debug logs.
interview_questions.example: before insert Opportunity trigger calling Http.send.
follow_ups: Timeout: cite 120 seconds max as documented for Apex callouts, not as a business SLA
weak_answer_warnings: Retrying the same sync trigger callout in a loop

interview_questions.question: How do you keep automation architecture Easy after go-live?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: One orchestrator per concern, named owners, tests, and an inventory. No silent extra Flow beside a trigger.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Intentional readability is an Easy attribute. I prefer a documented Flow plus small invocables over a mystery trigger farm. I schedule reviews when entry conditions change. I treat managed-package automations as extra cooks I must inventory. I do not equate Easy with 'no Apex ever.'
interview_questions.example: LAB_ object with a one-page automation map in the design record.
tradeoffs: Many tiny flows vs one large flow
follow_ups: What is a trigger framework's place? (Later APEX.)

interview_questions.question: Teach the Flow/Apex boundary with the kitchen brigade, then break the analogy.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Recipe cards are formula and validation, sign-off is approval, line cooks are Flow, pastry chef is Apex, the pass is order of execution, two cooks are duplicates. Callouts and legacy workflow break the picture.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk the five LAB_Opportunity needs. I say Apex is not a promotion; it is a technique the cards cannot express. I forbid invented limit numbers. I open the official pass-window page. I note Easy: the night shift must still read the recipe. I never use a library or labeled-drawer story.
interview_questions.example: Stamp, lost reason, approval, task, credit callout.
tradeoffs: Memorable analogy vs platform timing rules
weak_answer_warnings: A generic catalog metaphor instead of the kitchen-pass story
